title: Get the Middle East out of my politics!
gist: Smith argues the US should structurally disengage from the Middle East — militarily, diplomatically, and in domestic politics — because the oil rationale has collapsed: the US is a net oil exporter, the economy is a third to half as oil-sensitive as in the 1970s, and even Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz plus Trump's blockade of Iranian oil has failed to push crude back to its early-2010s highs. He also reads the polling collapse of Mamdani, El-Sayed and Netanyahu as evidence American voters want Middle Eastern politics out of US domestic races.

themes.theme: Polling signal: Middle East association is politically toxic

insights.claim: In a Harvard Harris poll of US political figures, only RFK Jr., Marco Rubio, and Mark Carney had net positive approval ratings, while Abdul El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani, and Benjamin Netanyahu scored below almost any American politician.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A cross-partisan approval floor for Middle East-identified figures is a leading indicator that Israel/Palestine positioning is a net negative in 2026-28 US races.
insights.locator: The other day I saw a Harvard Harris poll

insights.claim: The single trait shared by the three most unpopular figures in the poll is association with the intrusion of Middle Eastern politics into American politics, suggesting Americans simply want nothing to do with the region.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames a political-risk screen: candidates and PACs anchored on Middle East issues face a structural approval ceiling regardless of ideology.

insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If Israel/Palestine rather than economics drove a major-city mayoral win, expect that playbook to be replicated in urban primaries — and to draw offsetting AIPAC money.

themes.theme: Middle East politics colonizing US domestic races

insights.claim: Organizations linked to the Muslim Brotherhood such as CAIR Action are now recruiting and backing political candidates across the US using the Palestine issue, while AIPAC and other Israel-supporting groups pour money into the same races to stop them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An escalating two-sided money war in down-ballot US races raises the volatility of policy outcomes in states with concentrated Muslim or Jewish electorates.
insights.locator: Organizations like CAIR Action

insights.claim: Mobilizing Muslim and Jewish voters around Israel/Palestine rather than broad American issues actively fuels rightist attacks on both groups — the foreign-issue focus is self-harming for the constituencies pushing it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Second-order: identity-bloc mobilization on a foreign conflict increases domestic backlash risk, a tail risk for civil-liberties-sensitive policy.
insights.quote: provides fuel for rightist attacks on both groups
insights.locator: Furthermore, mobilizing Muslim and Jewish voters

insights.claim: Democrats should nominate candidates on Trump-opposition and issues of direct American relevance — Trump's corruption and authoritarianism, inflation, AI — rather than on Israel/Palestine positioning.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals the emerging center-left message discipline fight heading into 2026-28; a Palestine-centric Democratic primary field is a headwind to party competitiveness.
insights.quote: We should not be nominating Democratic politicians based on whether they support Israel or Palestine
insights.locator: This is simply bad for America

insights.claim: The post-9/11 era of heavy US Middle East involvement — Iraq, ISIS, the War on Terror, expanded Israel support, larger regional military presence, and now the Iran war — has on net been a disaster for US power and prestige and should be ended.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A grand-strategy pivot away from CENTCOM toward Asia would reshape defense procurement priorities and regional risk premia.
insights.quote: the era of heavy U.S. involvement in the Middle East has been a disaster for U.S. power and prestige, and it’s time for that era to end.
insights.locator: But overall, the era of heavy U.S. involvement

insights.claim: The War on Terror including the fight against ISIS was generally successful and necessary — a carve-out that distinguishes this disengagement case from the leftist 'blowback' critique of 9/11, which Smith explicitly rejects.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Disengagement advocacy from a hawkish-on-terror premise is more politically durable than left-isolationist framing — a more likely bipartisan policy path.
insights.quote: the War on Terror, including the fight against ISIS, was generally successful and necessary
insights.locator: I don’t believe that all of that involvement was a bad idea

insights.claim: Trump's Iran war continues to waste US military resources and make the US look weak while failing to accomplish any significant objective, and strong majorities of Americans polled say it is not worth fighting.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Domestic political support for the Iran conflict is already broken; de-escalation or drawdown is a live scenario that would compress oil risk premium further.
insights.quote: Recent polls show that a very strong majority of Americans think that the Iran War is not worth fighting.
insights.locator: Most obviously, there’s Trump’s disastrous war in Iran

insights.claim: Disengagement is far more feasible now than ten or twenty years ago because two pillars of the interventionist case have weakened simultaneously: Middle Eastern oil matters less to the global economy, and Islamism has generally declined after a successful War on Terror.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The structural case for US regional withdrawal is strengthening — price in lower US willingness to defend Gulf shipping lanes over the medium term.
insights.quote: The Iran War has shown that Middle Eastern oil is a lot less important for the global economy than it used to be.
insights.locator: Fortunately, conditions in the world have shifted

insights.claim: The Middle East's historic strategic value rested on low extraction costs making it the world's swing producer, so supply disruptions there could spike global prices and endanger industrialized economies — the logic that drove US intervention against Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the swing-producer premise no longer binds, the security rationale for a permanent Gulf military presence loses its economic anchor.
insights.quote: its low extraction costs mean it functions as the world’s “swing producer”
insights.locator: The U.S. doesn’t need to protect Middle Eastern oil supplies anymore

insights.claim: Blanchard and Gali (2007) found the 2000s US economy was only about a third to half as sensitive to oil prices as the 1970s economy, due to greater economic flexibility, better monetary policy that avoids printing money into a supply shock, and lower oil dependence.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The canonical elasticity to use when sizing oil-shock inflation and GDP scenarios; halves the implied macro damage of any Gulf supply disruption.
insights.quote: the economy of the 2000s was only about a third to half as sensitive to the price of oil as the economy of the 1970s had been
insights.locator: Blanchard and Gali (2007) looked at economic responses

insights.claim: Under Blanchard-Gali elasticities, a 10% oil price increase adds only about 0.25 percentage points to CPI and subtracts about 0.3 percentage points from GDP over roughly a year.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Concrete transfer function for trading oil-shock macro: a 10% crude move is a rounding error in headline inflation, not a policy-forcing event.
insights.quote: a 10% increase in the price of oil now (or at least, if “the 2000s” means “now”) leads to only a 0.25 percentage point increase in the CPI and a 0.3 percentage point reduction in GDP over the course of a year or so.
insights.locator: By their estimates, a 10% increase in the price of oil

insights.claim: Applying those elasticities to the roughly 50% oil spike around the Iran war's start implied inflation rising about 1.25 points to around 4% and GDP growth falling about 1.5 points to around 1.5% — described as frustrating and annoying, but not catastrophic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A pre-registered scenario to score: if realized inflation ran below ~4%, oil-shock transmission is even weaker than the model implies.
insights.quote: That would mean inflation would go to around 4% and GDP growth might go down to 1.5% — frustrating and annoying, but not catastrophic
insights.locator: Since oil just spiked by 50%

insights.claim: The US is now a net oil exporter, so when oil prices rise the gain to the domestic energy sector offsets at least part of the harm to other sectors — a structural dampener absent in prior oil shocks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US net-export status makes domestic energy equities a partial hedge against oil-driven macro drag — the shock is now a sector rotation more than an aggregate hit.
insights.quote: the U.S. is now a net oil exporter
insights.locator: In addition to having a more flexible economy

insights.claim: Despite Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz and Trump's retaliatory blockade of Iranian oil shipments, oil prices have not even regained their early-2010s highs, and in real terms — barrels priced in hours of average production-worker earnings — prices are not high at all.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The most extreme geopolitical supply event available failed to produce a price shock — argues for structurally lower geopolitical risk premium in crude.
insights.quote: Despite Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump’s retaliatory blockade of Iranian oil shipments, oil prices haven’t even reattained their highs from the early 2010s
insights.locator: But on top of all that, the fact is that the Iran War

insights.claim: US inflation has risen only slightly through the Iran war, and some of even that increase may be attributable to data-center boom demand rather than energy prices.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Attributing part of current inflation to AI data-center demand rather than oil changes which Fed reaction function assumptions apply.
insights.quote: inflation has only risen a little bit (and some of that may be due to demand from the data center boom)
insights.locator: No wonder the U.S. economy is still doing fine

insights.claim: Känzig and Raghavan (2025) examined the closure of key shipping chokepoints and produced similarly modest estimates of macroeconomic impact.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Independent corroboration that chokepoint closures are less macro-consequential than headline risk implies — useful against freight/energy panic trades.
insights.locator: Other estimates seem similarly modest

insights.claim: Smith has advocated Middle East disengagement and an Asia pivot since at least February 2021, writing then that the US 'will never be able to ignore the Middle East entirely, but we can remove ourselves much more than we've done' — and now considers the case far more urgent.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A long-held, consistent position rather than a reaction to current events — raises the weight of the forecast and signals durable elite drift toward Asia-first strategy.
insights.quote: [W]e need to draw down engagement in the Middle East, and increase engagement in Asia.
